seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 102 HTS Chapter 26 lines — iron ore, copper and lead concentrates, bauxite, manganese, uranium, molybdenum, tungsten, titanium ores, slag and ash. Most ores are Free and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs; who pays 10–37.5%, and why copper ore is outside the Section 232 copper tariff.

overview.intro:
Chapter 26 covers metal ores and concentrates — iron ore (2601), manganese, copper, nickel, cobalt, bauxite, lead, zinc, tin, chromium, tungsten, uranium and thorium, molybdenum, titanium, niobium, tantalum, vanadium, zirconium and precious-metal ores (2602–2617) — plus slag, ash and metal-bearing residues (2618–2621). **72 of the 102 tariff lines are Free**; the other 30 carry small duties charged on the **metal content** found by assay (for example 1.7¢/kg on the lead in copper concentrate), and most of those are Free for Australia, Chile, Peru, Canada, Mexico and other FTA partners. The U.S. imported **$3.85B** of Chapter 26 goods in 2025, led by uranium ore ($752M), iron ore pellets ($731M) and molybdenum ores.

The extra duties depend on the product. **Most ores are on the exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 tariffs** (U.S. note 52(b)): unagglomerated iron ore, manganese, copper, nickel, cobalt, bauxite, zinc, tin, chromium, tungsten, uranium, titanium and other ores pay nothing extra from any of the 60 economies. **Iron ore pellets, lead ore, roasted molybdenum, zirconium ore, gold ores, slag and most residues are not exempt** and pay 10% or 12.5% (Brazil up to 37.5%). China-origin goods pay 25% on most lines under the older Section 301 lists. Copper ores and concentrates are **not** covered by the Section 232 copper tariff, and the 2026 Section 232 critical-minerals action set no tariff. The IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026.

productGroups.label: Iron ore & concentrates
productGroups.blurb: Iron ore fines and concentrates (2601.11), pellets and other agglomerated ore (2601.12) and roasted pyrites: 7 lines, all Free. Unagglomerated ore is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; pellets are not, so pellets pay 10–12.5% (Canada 10% unless USMCA).

productGroups.label: Manganese ore
productGroups.blurb: Manganese ores and concentrates (including ferruginous ore with 20% or more manganese): 2 lines, Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. China-origin ore pays 25% (2024 four-year review).

productGroups.label: Copper ore & concentrates
productGroups.blurb: Copper ores and concentrates: 1.7¢/kg on the lead content (Free for USMCA, FTA and AGOA goods), reported by copper, lead, zinc, silver and gold content. Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty and outside the Section 232 copper tariff.

productGroups.label: Nickel ore
productGroups.blurb: Nickel ores and concentrates: 2 lines, Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Cobalt ore
productGroups.blurb: Cobalt ores and concentrates: 1 line, Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. China-origin ore pays 25%.

productGroups.label: Bauxite (aluminum ore)
productGroups.blurb: Bauxite and other aluminum ores — calcined bauxite (refractory grade and other) and other: 3 lines, Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. Guyana and Jamaica were the main suppliers in 2025.

productGroups.label: Lead ore & concentrates
productGroups.blurb: Lead ores and concentrates: 1.1¢/kg on lead content. Not on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list, so non-USMCA Canadian ore pays +10% and FTA partners such as Australia +12.5% even when the base rate is Free.

productGroups.label: Zinc ore & concentrates
productGroups.blurb: Zinc ores and concentrates: 5 lines (by metal content), Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. China-origin ore pays 25%.

productGroups.label: Tin ore
productGroups.blurb: Tin ores and concentrates: 1 line, Free, and no extra duty from any origin — not even China.

productGroups.label: Chromium ore (chromite)
productGroups.blurb: Chromium ores and concentrates (chromite), split by Cr2O3 content: 3 lines, Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. South Africa is the main supplier.

productGroups.label: Tungsten ore & concentrates
productGroups.blurb: Tungsten ores (Free) and concentrates (37.5¢/kg on tungsten content; Free for FTA and AGOA goods). Both are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; Chinese concentrates pay +25% (2024 four-year review).

productGroups.label: Uranium & thorium ore
productGroups.blurb: Uranium ores and concentrates (2612.10) and thorium ores (2612.20): Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. The largest Chapter 26 import in 2025, from Australia and Namibia. NRC import rules apply.

productGroups.label: Molybdenum ore & concentrates
productGroups.blurb: Molybdenum ores and concentrates: roasted (2613.10, 12.8¢/kg on Mo content + 1.8%) and other (2613.90, 17.8¢/kg on Mo content). Unroasted concentrate is exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; roasted is not.
productGroups.rateSummary: 12.8¢/kg on molybdenum content + 1.8% · 17.8¢/kg on molybdenum content

productGroups.label: Titanium ore (ilmenite, rutile)
productGroups.blurb: Titanium ores: synthetic rutile, ilmenite and ilmenite sand, rutile: 3 lines, Free, exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Niobium, tantalum, vanadium & zirconium ores
productGroups.blurb: Zirconium ores (zircon, 2615.10) and niobium, tantalum and vanadium ores (2615.90): all Free. Zirconium ore is not on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list; the others are.

productGroups.label: Silver, gold & other precious-metal ores
productGroups.blurb: Silver ores (0.8¢/kg on lead content) and gold and other precious-metal ores (1.7¢/kg on lead content), reported by metal content. Silver ores are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; gold ores are not.
productGroups.rateSummary: 0.8¢/kg on lead content · 1.7¢/kg on lead content

productGroups.label: Other ores (antimony, beryllium)
productGroups.blurb: Antimony ores (exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty) and other ores such as beryllium ores (not exempt): 3 lines, all Free.

productGroups.label: Granulated slag (slag sand)
productGroups.blurb: Granulated blast-furnace slag (slag sand) from iron or steel making, used in cement: 1 line, Free, but not exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Iron & steel slag, dross & scale
productGroups.blurb: Other iron and steel slag, dross, mill scale and waste: 2 lines, Free, not exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

productGroups.label: Metal-bearing slag, ash & residues
productGroups.blurb: Slag, ash and residues containing metals (zinc dross, copper and lead residues, leaded gasoline sludge, arsenic and vanadium residues, titanium slag): 36 lines, mostly Free. Only copper residues (2620.30) and titanium slag (2620.99.50) are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.
productGroups.rateSummary: Free · 0.7¢/kg on copper content + 0.7¢/kg on lead content · 5% · 17.6¢/kg on tungsten content + 3.8%

productGroups.label: Other slag & ash (incinerator ash, kelp)
productGroups.blurb: Ash and residues from incinerating municipal waste and other slag and ash, including seaweed ash (kelp): 2 lines, Free, not exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

workedExamples.title: 10,000 t of copper concentrate
workedExamples.body: Copper concentrate pays **1.7¢/kg on its lead content**, less an allowance of 18 kg per dry metric ton (Chapter 26 additional U.S. note 1). A concentrate with 0.5% lead holds 50 kg of lead per dry ton, so 32 kg is dutiable: 10,000 t × 32 kg × $0.017 = **$5,440**. From Chile, Peru, Australia, Canada or Mexico (FTA or USMCA claim) the duty is **$0**. 2603.00.00 is on the U.S. note 52(b) list, so no 2026 Section 301 duty applies, and Proclamation 10962 (Section 232 copper) does not cover ores or concentrates.

workedExamples.title: $10 million of iron ore pellets: Brazil vs Canada
workedExamples.body: Pellets are Free, but 2601.12 is not on the note 52(b) exemption list. Brazilian pellets pay the **12.5%** 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.27) = **$1.25 million**; they are on the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)), so the separate 25% Brazil duty does not apply. Canadian pellets pay **$0** with a USMCA claim (9903.05.93), otherwise **10%** = $1 million. Unagglomerated iron ore fines (2601.11) are exempt and pay $0 from either country.

workedExamples.title: Molybdenum concentrate from Peru vs roasted moly from Chile
workedExamples.body: Unroasted molybdenum concentrate (2613.90) pays 17.8¢/kg on molybdenum content, but the Peru TPA rate is **Free** and 2613.90 is on the note 52(b) list, so Peruvian concentrate pays **$0**. Roasted molybdenum concentrate (2613.10) from Chile is also Free under the FTA, but 2613.10 is not on the exemption list and the 2026 Section 301 duty applies even when an FTA rate is claimed (note 52(a)): **12.5%** of value, $125,000 on a $1 million lot.

workedExamples.title: Tungsten concentrate from China
workedExamples.body: Tungsten concentrates pay 37.5¢/kg on tungsten content plus **25%** for China (9903.91.01, the 2024 four-year review, since September 27, 2024). 1,000 kg of contained tungsten worth $40,000 pays $375 + $10,000 = **$10,375**. The 2026 Section 301 duty does not apply (note 52(b)). Tungsten ores (2611.00.30) from China pay only their Free base rate.

**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) slag or similar industrial waste prepared as macadam (heading 2517); (b) natural magnesium carbonate (magnesite), whether or not calcined (heading 2519); (c) sludges from the storage tanks of petroleum oils, consisting mainly of such oils (heading 2710); (d) basic slag of chapter 31; (e) slag wool, rock wool or similar mineral wools (heading 6806); (f) waste or scrap of precious metal or of metal clad with precious metal; other waste or scrap containing precious metal or precious metal compounds, of a kind used principally for the recovery of precious metal (heading 7112 or 8549); or (g) copper, nickel or cobalt mattes produced by any process of smelting (section XV).

**Note 2.** For the purposes of headings 2601 to 2617, the term "ores" means minerals of mineralogical species actually used in the metallurgical industry for the extraction of mercury, of the metals of heading 2844 or of the metals of section XIV or XV, even if they are intended for non-metallurgical purposes. Headings 2601 to 2617 do not, however, include minerals which have been submitted to processes not normal to the metallurgical industry.

**Note 3.** Heading 2620 applies only to: (a) slag, ash and residues of a kind used in industry either for the extraction of metals or as a basis for the manufacture of chemical compounds of metals, excluding ash and residues from the incineration of municipal waste (heading 2621); and (b) slag, ash and residues containing arsenic, whether or not containing metals, of a kind used either for the extraction of arsenic or metals or for the manufacture of their chemical compounds.

**Subheading note 1.** For the purposes of subheading 2620.21, "leaded gasoline sludges and leaded anti-knock compound sludges" means sludges obtained from storage tanks of leaded gasoline and leaded anti-knock compounds (for example, tetraethyl lead), and consisting essentially of lead, lead compounds and iron oxide.

**Subheading note 2.** Slag, ash and residues containing arsenic, mercury, thallium or their mixtures, of a kind used for the extraction of arsenic or those metals or for the manufacture of their chemical compounds, are to be classified in subheading 2620.60.

**Note 1.** The specific rates of duty imposed under the headings of this chapter on the metal content of ores and other materials shall apply to the assay quantity of metal contained therein, whether recovered as metals, as alloys or as chemical compounds or used directly in the manufacture of articles, except that with respect to ores or other materials provided for in this chapter which are subject to duty at specific rates on their copper, lead or zinc content, an absolute deduction for losses of 18 kg per dry metric ton from the respective quantities of each of such metal contents shall be allowed.

**Note 2.** When the classification of imported materials under any provision of this chapter is dependent on the percentage of metal content, such percentage shall be the ratio of the total quantity of the respective metal content to the total quantity of imported material when computed on a dry-weight basis; i.e., free of all uncombined moisture.

**Statistical notes.** The quantity of metal content to be reported is the assay quantity without deductions. "Coarse" iron ore (2601.11.0060) has a majority of particles over 4.75 mm. For the 10-digit lines under 2603.00.00, 2604.00.00, 2607.00.00, 2608.00.00, 2616.10.00, 2616.90.00, 2620.19.60, 2620.21.00, 2620.29.00 and 2620.30.00, and 2620.99.7560 and 2620.99.7580, the weight and value of each named metal in the shipment is reported under its own statistical number, so one shipment can need several 10-digit lines.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 26: Ores, Slag and Ash — Tariff Updates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 26 Tariff Updates 2025–2026: Iron Ore, Copper Ore, Critical Minerals, Section 301 & 232 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for imports of ores, slag and ash since January 2025: the IEEPA tariffs and their end, the Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs and the note 52(b) ore exemption, Brazil and China duties, the Section 232 copper and critical-minerals actions — with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 102 Chapter 26 lines have the same base rates in both — the changes were extra duties.

In 2025 the IEEPA tariffs reached ores from Canada and Mexico (non-USMCA goods; energy and critical minerals of Canada at 10%), China, Brazil and, through the April 2025 reciprocal tariff, every other country — but most ores were on the reciprocal tariff's exemption list. Iron ore, lead ore, slag and ash were not. **All IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026.** A 10% Section 122 surcharge with the same ore exemptions ran until July 23, 2026.

Today's extra duties are the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** on 60 economies (10% or 12.5%, from July 24, 2026), which exempt most ores under U.S. note 52(b) but charge iron ore pellets, lead ore, roasted molybdenum, zirconium ore, gold ores, slag, ash and most residues; Brazil's 25% Section 301 duty; and the **China Section 301** duties (25% on most lines). Copper ores are outside the Section 232 copper tariff, and the January 2026 Section 232 critical-minerals proclamation imposed no tariff.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 26 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their U.S. note 52(b) exemption list, the Brazil and China Section 301 actions, Russia's column 2 and 35% rates, the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties, and the Section 232 copper and critical-minerals actions (which set no Chapter 26 tariff). We found no antidumping or countervailing duty order on Chapter 26 goods. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 26 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 102 Chapter 26 tariff lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), with no ore exemption. The rate is 0% in 2026. Nicaragua shipped no Chapter 26 goods to the U.S. in 2025.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries and remain in effect pending the statutory review. The 25% List 3 and 2024 four-year-review duties on Chinese ores continue.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: most ores exempt
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect on July 24, 2026. 23 Chapter 26 subheadings (50 lines) are on the U.S. note 52(b) exemption list (9903.05.86). The other 52 lines pay: iron ore pellets, lead ore, roasted molybdenum, zirconium ore, gold and other precious-metal ores, beryllium ores, granulated slag, steel slag and scale, most metal-bearing residues and incinerator ash. USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt; EU and Japan goods pay 10% and 12.5% in total.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. Its exemption list (9903.03.03) had the note 52(b) ores except iron ore; iron ore, lead ore, slag, ash and residues paid it.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301 tariff: 25%, most ores exempt
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect July 22, 2026. Its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03) covers the same ores as note 52(b) plus iron ore pellets (2601.12), but not roasted pyrites (2601.20). Brazilian pellets therefore pay only the 12.5% 60-economy duty; slag, lead ore and residues pay both (37.5%).

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: AGOA duty-free treatment extended through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: Proclamation 11030 implemented the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026: AGOA (SPI D) applies through December 31, 2026, and Gabon was re-designated a beneficiary. South Africa, Namibia, Madagascar, Mozambique and Sierra Leone are listed beneficiaries (general note 16). For Chapter 26 this makes the content-duty lines (copper, lead, tungsten, molybdenum, precious-metal ores and residues) Free for qualifying goods.

changes.title: USTR consults on a plurilateral critical-minerals agreement
changes.detail: Following Proclamation 11001, USTR requested comments on the design of a plurilateral agreement on trade in critical minerals and on policy actions such as price floors. No tariff has been set on critical-mineral ores.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; most ores exempt
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Most non-ferrous ores (the note 52(b) list without iron ore) were exempt (9903.03.03), as were USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico. Iron ore, lead ore, slag, ash and residues paid.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24.

changes.title: Section 232 critical minerals: negotiations, no tariff
changes.detail: Proclamation 11001 concurred that imports of processed critical minerals and their derivative products threaten national security, but directed Commerce and USTR to negotiate agreements (considering price floors) instead of imposing tariffs, with an update due within 180 days. No Chapter 26 line pays a Section 232 duty.

changes.title: IEEPA 40% duty on Brazil; iron ore and tin ore exempt
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on products of Brazil (9903.01.77). Iron ore (2601.11, 2601.12) and tin ore (2609) were on its exemption list (9903.01.81); iron ore still paid the 10% reciprocal tariff. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10); energy and critical minerals (9903.01.13) stayed at 10%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 copper tariff does not cover ores
changes.detail: Proclamation 10962 imposed 50% on semi-finished copper products and copper-intensive derivatives from August 1, 2025. Copper ores and concentrates (2603) are not covered; a phased tariff on refined copper (15% in 2027, 30% in 2028) was left for a later decision after a Commerce update due June 30, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff: most ores exempt, iron ore and slag not
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico, from April 5, 2025. Manganese, copper, cobalt, bauxite, zinc, chromium, tungsten, uranium, titanium, niobium/tantalum/vanadium, silver and antimony ores were on the Annex II exemption list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)); nickel, tin, thorium and unroasted molybdenum ores were added later in 2025. Iron ore, lead ore, slag, ash and most residues paid. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025, with 10% for Canadian energy and critical minerals as defined by 30 U.S.C. 1606(a)(3) (9903.01.13). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China: 25% on critical-mineral ores (four-year review)
changes.detail: USTR's four-year review added a 25% duty (9903.91.01) on Chinese manganese, cobalt, aluminum, zinc and chromium ores and tungsten concentrates, among other critical minerals.

changes.title: Russia: 35% on iron ore pellets and zirconium ore
changes.detail: Proclamation 10523 added iron ore pellets (2601.12) and zirconium ores (2615.10) of Russia to the list paying 35% in place of the column 2 rate (9903.90.08, U.S. note 30(b)).

changes.title: China List 4A on incinerator ash cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: The List 4A duty (9903.88.15) on Chinese ash and residues from municipal waste incineration (2621.10), imposed at 15% from September 1, 2019, was cut to 7.5%.

changes.title: China List 3 raised to 25%
changes.detail: List 3 (9903.88.03), which covers 73 Chapter 26 lines including iron ore, nickel, titanium, uranium ores, slag and residues, rose from 10% (from September 24, 2018) to 25%.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 26 goods were **$3.85B in 2025**, +5.7% from $3.64B in 2024 and up from $2.29B in 2020. Each heading has its own supplier: **uranium ores** ($752M) came from Australia ($605M) and Namibia ($147M); **iron ore** ($783M) from Brazil ($381M) and Canada ($329M); **molybdenum** ($660M) from Peru ($346M) and Mexico ($268M); **titanium ores** ($424M) from South Africa, Australia, Madagascar, Mozambique and Sierra Leone; **bauxite** ($161M) from Guyana and Jamaica; **manganese** from Gabon; **chromite** from South Africa; and **lead concentrate** ($120M) from Canada. Metal-bearing residues ($350M) come mainly from South Africa, Norway and Canada, and granulated slag ($178M) from Japan, China and South Africa.

Copper is the notable gap: imports of copper ores and concentrates were only $660K. Mexico's shipments more than doubled to $331M on molybdenum, and Chile's fell to $63.3M. Most ores were exempt from the 2025 reciprocal tariff; among the lines that paid it, granulated slag fell to $178M from $268M and iron ore pellets to $731M from $782M.

Many of these ores have no large U.S. mine supply: the USGS puts 2025 U.S. net import reliance at 100% for manganese, niobium and tantalum, 88% for titanium mineral concentrates, 79% for chromium and over 75% for bauxite, but under 25% for zirconium ores (Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, Figure 2).

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. For most ores the answer is **Free**: they are on the exemption list of the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)). The lines that pay are **iron ore pellets, lead ore, roasted molybdenum, zircon, gold ores, slag, ash and residues** — 10% for Canada, Mexico (without USMCA) and the EU, 12.5% for Australia, Peru, Chile, South Africa, Norway and Japan, and up to 37.5% for Brazil. **China** pays 25% on most ores and 37.5% on slag and residues.

Content-based base rates (cents per kg of lead, tungsten or molybdenum) are shown as written; FTA, USMCA and AGOA claims make them Free. **Russia** pays the column 2 rates, 35% on pellets and zircon, and 12.5% on top on non-exempt lines.

Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.

Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; AU for Australia; D for South Africa; PE for Peru; D for Namibia; D for Madagascar; CL for Chile. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.

No Section 232 duty is applied: Proclamation 10962 (copper) does not cover ores or concentrates, and Proclamation 11001 (processed critical minerals) set no tariff. We found no antidumping or countervailing duty order on Chapter 26 goods.
AGOA (SPI D) is in force through December 31, 2026 and is applied for South Africa, Namibia and Madagascar; other sub-Saharan beneficiaries (e.g. Gabon, Mozambique, Sierra Leone) can claim it too.
Content-based rates are charged on the assay quantity of metal; for copper, lead and zinc content, 18 kg per dry metric ton is deducted (Chapter 26 additional U.S. note 1).
Russia is priced at the column 2 rates (normal trade relations suspended), with 35% in place of column 2 on iron ore pellets and zirconium ore (9903.90.08) and 12.5% on non-exempt lines.
Entry rules still apply: uranium and thorium ores need an NRC-authorized consignee (10 CFR 110.27), and hazardous-waste residues and ash need EPA import consent (40 CFR 262.84).

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 26: Ores, Slag and Ash — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Ores & Concentrates: NRC, EPA & CBP Assay Rules and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 26) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 26 line — CBP sampling and assay of metal-bearing ores, TSCA certification, NRC licensing for uranium and thorium ores, EPA consent for hazardous residues and ash — and the legal ways to pay less: FTA, USMCA and AGOA claims, the 18 kg/t deduction, bonded smelting warehouses and drawback.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 26 ores are **Free**, so the duty you can save comes from three places: the **metal-content duties** on copper, lead, tungsten, molybdenum and precious-metal ores (Free with an FTA, USMCA or AGOA claim), the **10–12.5% Section 301 duty** on iron ore pellets, lead ore, slag and residues (avoided by USMCA claims or by buying from countries outside the 60 economies), and the **China** duties.

The paperwork follows the material: every metal-bearing ore is sampled and assayed for CBP, chemical substances need a TSCA certification, uranium and thorium ores are NRC source material, and residues or ash that are hazardous waste need EPA consent before they ship. Each rule and lever below links to its regulation.

levers.title: Claim the FTA, USMCA or AGOA rate on the metal-content duties
levers.saves: The whole base duty on the 30 dutiable lines — e.g. 1.7¢/kg of lead content on copper concentrate, 37.5¢/kg of tungsten, 17.8¢/kg of molybdenum
levers.appliesTo: Copper, lead, tungsten, molybdenum and precious-metal ores and the dutiable residues (2620.19.60, 2620.60.10, 2620.99.20), from Australia, Chile, Peru, Korea, Colombia, Canada, Mexico and other FTA partners, or AGOA beneficiaries
levers.document: The FTA claim on the entry (SPI AU, CL, PE, KR, CO …) with the supporting certification or importer knowledge required by the agreement; for AGOA, SPI D and goods of a beneficiary country listed in general note 16.
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duty still applies when an FTA rate is claimed (U.S. note 52(a)). AGOA runs through December 31, 2026; GSP (A, A+, A*) has lapsed.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican ore, slag and residues
levers.saves: 10% of value on the 52 lines not on note 52(b) (iron ore pellets, lead ore, roasted molybdenum, slag, residues), plus the content-based base rates
levers.appliesTo: The 30 lines with a base-rate duty and the 52 lines not on note 52(b) (64 lines in all), for originating goods of Canada or Mexico
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer; it need not follow a prescribed format and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Ore mined in Canada or Mexico is wholly obtained and originates; check slag and residues against the rules of origin. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Buy non-exempt products from a country outside the 60 Section 301 economies
levers.saves: 10% or 12.5% of value (Brazil up to 37.5%, China 25–37.5%) on iron ore pellets, lead ore, zircon, gold ores, slag, ash and residues
levers.appliesTo: The 52 lines not on the U.S. note 52(b) exemption list
levers.document: Commercial invoice, mine or smelter records and bill of lading showing where the ore was mined or the slag produced.
levers.caveat: Origin is where the ore was mined; blending or transshipment through a third country does not change it. Exempt ores (most of the chapter) pay nothing extra from any of the 60 economies anyway.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52

levers.title: Pay on the assayed metal content — and take the 18 kg/t deduction
levers.saves: Duty on metal that is not there: content rates apply to the assay quantity, and copper, lead and zinc content is reduced by 18 kg per dry metric ton
levers.appliesTo: Lines with a rate on metal content (copper, lead, tungsten, molybdenum and precious-metal ores; 2620.19.60, 2620.99.20)
levers.document: Representative moisture and assay samples taken under CBP supervision (or a verified commercial sample), with the assay results on the entry.
levers.caveat: CBP liquidates on its own laboratory assay when it tests the sample. The 18 kg deduction is allowed only if the importer followed the procedures (19 CFR 151.55).

levers.title: Smelt or refine in a bonded smelting and refining warehouse
levers.saves: The content duty on dutiable metal that is exported (charges against the bond are credited on export), and deferral until metal is withdrawn for consumption
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable metal-bearing ores and residues smelted or refined to unwrought metal or oxides
levers.document: Application to the port director to bond the plant, a smelting and refining bond, and warehouse entries with weight, sampling and assay records.
levers.caveat: Covers the base (metal-content) duties under section 312 of the Tariff Act; we found no guidance that it removes Section 301 duties. Wastage allowances are set per plant.

levers.title: Claim drawback when imported ore or slag is exported or used in exported goods
levers.saves: Up to 99% of duties paid — including Section 301 duties on Chinese ores — on goods exported or used to make exported products
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refundable as drawback; claims have strict time limits and record requirements.

rules.title: Metal-bearing ores and materials: sampled for moisture and assay at the port of first arrival (or moved under bond to a sampling plant)
Report the weight and value of each named metal (copper, lead, zinc, silver, gold …) under its own 10-digit line; one shipment can need several lines
TSCA import certification (positive or negative) for chemical substances at entry

Uranium and thorium ores are source material: imported under the general license only if the U.S. consignee is authorized by an NRC or Agreement State license (unprocessed ore may be held but not processed without one)

Uranium and thorium ores and concentrates intended for processing are Class 7 (radioactive) in transport; natural ores not processed for their radionuclides are excepted below 10 times the exempt activity
Slag, ash, sludge and residues that are hazardous waste: importer notification, EPA consent, contract and manifest before shipment

groups.label: Iron ore & concentrates
groups.note: Pellets (2601.12) pay the 2026 Section 301 duty and, from Russia, 35%; ore fines and concentrate (2601.11) are exempt. Report tonnage by coarse, concentrate and other.

groups.label: Manganese ore
groups.note: Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; China-origin ore pays 25% (2024 review). Classification at 20% or more manganese is on a dry-weight basis (additional U.S. note 2).

groups.label: Copper ore & concentrates
groups.note: Duty is on the lead content (18 kg/t deduction); report copper, lead, zinc, silver and gold content under separate lines. Not covered by the Section 232 copper tariff.

groups.label: Nickel ore
groups.note: Report nickel content and other metal content separately. Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

groups.label: Cobalt ore
groups.note: Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; China-origin ore pays 25%.

groups.label: Bauxite (aluminum ore)
groups.note: Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; China-origin bauxite pays 25%.

groups.label: Lead ore & concentrates
groups.note: Content duty on lead (18 kg/t deduction) and the 2026 Section 301 duty; claim USMCA for Canadian concentrate.

groups.label: Zinc ore & concentrates
groups.note: Report metal contents separately. Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; China-origin concentrate pays 25%.

groups.label: Tin ore
groups.note: No extra duty from any origin.

groups.label: Chromium ore (chromite)
groups.note: Lines split by Cr2O3 content. Exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; China-origin ore pays 25%.

groups.label: Tungsten ore & concentrates
groups.note: Concentrates pay 37.5¢/kg on tungsten content (Free under FTAs and AGOA); Chinese concentrates +25%.

groups.label: Uranium & thorium ore
groups.note: NRC: the U.S. consignee must hold an NRC or Agreement State license for source material; DOT Class 7 rules apply to ore for processing.

groups.label: Molybdenum ore & concentrates
groups.note: Unroasted concentrate exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; roasted (2613.10) pays it even with an FTA claim.

groups.label: Titanium ore (ilmenite, rutile)
groups.note: Mineral sands can contain thorium or uranium; at 0.05% or more by weight they are NRC source material.

groups.label: Niobium, tantalum, vanadium & zirconium ores
groups.note: Zircon (2615.10) pays the 2026 Section 301 duty and, from Russia, 35%. Tantalum and niobium ores can contain uranium or thorium (NRC rules at 0.05% or more).

groups.label: Silver, gold & other precious-metal ores
groups.note: Content duty on lead; report each precious metal. Silver ores exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, gold ores (2616.90) not.

groups.label: Other ores (antimony, beryllium)
groups.note: Antimony ores exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty; beryllium and other ores (2617.90) not.

groups.label: Granulated slag (slag sand)
groups.note: Pays the 2026 Section 301 duty (Japan and the EU 12.5% and 10% in total).

groups.label: Iron & steel slag, dross & scale
groups.note: Pays the 2026 Section 301 duty. Check whether the material is a hazardous waste before shipping.

groups.label: Metal-bearing slag, ash & residues
groups.note: Residues such as leaded gasoline sludge, arsenic or mercury residues can be hazardous waste (EPA consent). Only 2620.30 and 2620.99.50 are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.

groups.label: Other slag & ash (incinerator ash, kelp)
groups.note: Incinerator ash can be hazardous waste (EPA consent). Pays the 2026 Section 301 duty; Chinese ash 20%.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. Whether a residue is a hazardous waste, or an ore is NRC source material, depends on its composition; check with EPA, the NRC and CBP before importing.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on ores, concentrates, slag and ash — by product, by country and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: 72 of the 102 Chapter 26 lines are Free; the other 30 charge cents per kg of metal content, which FTA, USMCA and AGOA claims remove.

Most ores are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (U.S. note 52(b)); iron ore pellets, lead ore, roasted molybdenum, zircon, gold ores, slag, ash and residues pay 10–12.5% (Brazil up to 37.5%, USMCA goods exempt). China pays 25% on most ores.
No Section 232 tariff reaches Chapter 26: copper ores are outside the copper tariff and the January 2026 critical-minerals action set no tariff. The IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on iron ore?
faqs.answer: Iron ore is Free under the general rate, but the extra duty depends on its form. Ore fines and concentrate (2601.11) are on the U.S. note 52(b) list and pay nothing extra. Pellets and other agglomerated ore (2601.12) pay the 2026 Section 301 duty: 12.5% from Brazil, Australia or Chile, 10% from the EU, and 10% from Canada unless a USMCA claim is made. Chinese iron ore pays 25% or 37.5%, and Russian pellets 35% plus 12.5%.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import iron ore from?
searchedAs: where does the us import iron ore from
where does us get iron ore
faqs.answer: Mostly Brazil ($381M in 2025) and Canada ($329M), then Sweden and Chile. U.S. iron ore imports were $783M in 2025, nearly all pellets ($731M).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for iron ore pellets, fines and concentrate?
searchedAs: hs code for iron ore pellets
hs code for iron ore fines
hs code for iron ore concentrate
hs code of iron ore lumps
faqs.answer: 2601.11 is non-agglomerated iron ore — fines, lumps and concentrate (U.S. lines 2601.11.00.30 concentrates, .60 coarse, .90 other). 2601.12 is agglomerated ore: pellets (2601.12.00.30), briquettes (.60) and other (.90). Roasted iron pyrites is 2601.20. All are Free; only 2601.12 pays the 2026 Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on copper ore or copper concentrate?
faqs.answer: Copper ores and concentrates (2603.00.00) pay 1.7¢/kg on their lead content, less 18 kg per dry ton — Free from Chile, Peru, Australia, Canada, Mexico and other FTA partners. They are on the note 52(b) list, so no 2026 Section 301 duty applies, and the 50% Section 232 copper tariff (Proclamation 10962, August 1, 2025) covers semi-finished copper products and derivatives, not ores or concentrates. The U.S. imported only $0.7M of copper ores in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for copper ores and concentrates?
searchedAs: hs code for copper ores and concentrates
faqs.answer: 2603.00.00. The U.S. reports a shipment under five 10-digit lines by metal: copper content (2603.00.00.10), lead (.20), zinc (.30), silver (.40) and gold (.50), each with that metal's weight and value. Copper mattes and cement copper are 7401 (Chapter 74), not Chapter 26.

faqs.question: Are critical minerals exempt from tariffs?
searchedAs: are critical minerals exempt from tariffs
faqs.answer: Mostly, at the ore stage. Manganese, nickel, cobalt, bauxite, zinc, tin, chromium, tungsten, uranium, titanium, niobium, tantalum, vanadium and antimony ores are on the 2026 Section 301 exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)), as most were on the reciprocal tariff and Section 122 exemption lists. Zircon and beryllium ores are not, and China-origin ores pay 25% under Section 301 whatever the mineral. Processed critical minerals in Chapters 28, 81 and others have their own rates.

faqs.question: What happened with the Section 232 critical minerals investigation?
faqs.answer: Commerce began the investigation under Executive Order 14272 (April 15, 2025) and reported on October 24, 2025. In Proclamation 11001 of January 14, 2026 the President agreed that imports threaten national security but chose negotiations — with price floors to be considered — instead of tariffs, with an update due within 180 days. USTR asked for comments on a plurilateral critical-minerals agreement on February 26, 2026. No Section 232 duty applies to Chapter 26 ores.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on uranium?
faqs.answer: Uranium ores and concentrates (2612.10) are Free and on the note 52(b) exemption list, so Australian and Namibian supplies pay no tariff. Only China-origin ore pays (25%, List 3). Canadian uranium ore paid 10% under IEEPA in 2025 unless entered under USMCA, but that ended February 24, 2026. Uranium ore was the largest Chapter 26 import in 2025 ($752M). Importers need an NRC-authorized consignee (10 CFR 110.27).

faqs.question: Does the U.S. import uranium from Russia?
searchedAs: does the us import uranium from russia
does the us still import uranium from russia
does the us import enriched uranium from russia
what countries does the us import uranium from
faqs.answer: Not uranium ore: 2025 Chapter 26 uranium imports came from Australia and Namibia. The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act (Public Law 118-62, May 13, 2024) bans unirradiated low-enriched uranium produced in Russia from August 2024, with Energy Department waivers capped by annual quantities and ending no later than January 1, 2028.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on bauxite?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on bauxite
where does the us import bauxite from
where does the us get bauxite from
faqs.answer: No, except from China. Bauxite (2606.00.00) is Free and on the note 52(b) list, so it pays nothing extra from Guyana, Jamaica, Australia or Brazil; Chinese bauxite pays 25% (2024 four-year review). The U.S. imported $161M in 2025, mainly from Guyana ($63.7M) and Jamaica ($40.1M).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on tungsten ore from China?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on tungsten
faqs.answer: Tungsten concentrates (2611.00.60) pay 37.5¢/kg on tungsten content plus 25% for China (9903.91.01, since September 27, 2024). Tungsten ores (2611.00.30) are Free and on no China list. Both are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, and concentrates are Free from FTA partners such as Australia, Korea and Peru.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for slag?
searchedAs: hs code for granulated blast furnace slag
faqs.answer: Granulated blast-furnace slag (slag sand) is 2618.00.00; other iron and steel slag, dross and mill scale 2619.00; slag and residues used to recover other metals 2620 (copper residues 2620.30, zinc dross 2620.19.30, titanium slag 2620.99.50); incinerator and other ash 2621. Slag prepared as macadam is 2517 and slag wool 6806. All Chapter 26 slag lines are Free, but most pay the 2026 Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What are the HS codes for manganese, chrome, ilmenite, rutile and zircon?
faqs.answer: Manganese ore 2602.00.00; chromite (chrome ore) 2610.00.00, split by Cr2O3 content; ilmenite and ilmenite sand 2614.00.60.20; rutile and rutile sand 2614.00.60.40; synthetic rutile 2614.00.30; zircon (zirconium ore) 2615.10.00. All are Free; zircon is the only one not exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty.
